column88: On 19 Nov. 2021, the government of Canada continues to advise: “Testing is the only way we can confirm if you have COVID-19. Knowing you're infected is important to protect your family and the people you encounter. Contact your local health authority for advice about testing if you think you may have COVID-19 (and/or) have been in contact with someone who has COVID-19.” Provincial, territorial and local public health agencies follow this guidance to test individuals who report possible symptoms or are possible contacts. Lateral flow tests (LFTs) have been approved by Health Canada. While lateral flow tests (LFTs) and other rapid tests are increasingly available to some asymptomatic people in some provinces, PCR testing of symptomatic individuals remains the standard first-test approach in the majority of cases in addition to being relied upon for final confirmation. See Government of Canada, Globe and Mail and CBC news websites, archived:  https://web.archive.org/web/20211119145149/https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/2019-novel-coronavirus-infection/symptoms/testing.html  https://web.archive.org/web/20211119193116/https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-ontario-expanding-covid-19-testing-in-pharmacies-schools-and-mobile/  https://web.archive.org/web/20211006213204/https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/edmonton/alberta-to-resume-contact-tracing-in-schools-provide-rapid-testing-kits-to-families-1.62006
column90: As of 19 november 2021, government of Canada advises that when individuals “test positive for COVID-19, a public health official will ask you questions to collect important information about your symptoms; activities and travel you did before you tested positive; all the people you may have been in close contact with while you were contagious ...contact tracing. It's a key public health measure.” Most provinces and territories continue to apply this advice. However, the province of Alberta’s policy: “Individuals with positive tests will continue to be notified. Contact tracers will not notify close contacts of positive cases, but will ask that individuals do so when informed of their positive result. Contact tracers will continue to investigate cases in high-risk settings, such as acute and continuing care.” See Governments of Canada and Alberta websites, archived:  https://web.archive.org/web/20211119145149/https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/2019-novel-coronavirus-infection/symptoms/testing.html  https://web.archive.org/web/20211119152300/https://www.alberta.ca/covid-19-public-health-actions.aspx

column106: On 19 november 2021 11:10AM EST, according to the CTV news unofficial vaccine tracker, 30,029,781 Canadians [78.5% of the total national population and just under 90% of the vaccine-eligible population aged 12+] have received at least one dose of an approved COVID-19 vaccine -- Moderna, Pfizer, Johnson & Johnson (J&J) Janssen, or AstraZeneca (AZ no longer recommended except in limited circumstances). 28,785,773 Canadians [75% of total pop. and 86% of vax-eligible] are fully vaccinated against COVID-19 having received two doses. All provinces and territories are making vaccinations available to residents aged 12 and up or those born in 2009 and before with Moderna authorized 27 August 2021 for children aged 12-17 in addition to original authorization for 18+ and Pfizer already approved for 12-17 on 5 May 2021. Vaccinations for those aged 5-11 have been authorized, but not administered yet. Provinces and territories are also delivering third doses to long-term care residents, immune-compromised patients, indigenous community residents, senior citizens and recipients of two earlier AZ doses based on national government guidance. 709,912 third doses have been administered, which accounts for less than 2% of the national population. (Note that vaccination data do not include Canadians who returned home after being vaccinated in other countries while wintering at retirement homes or on essential business trips. On the other hand, there may be a small amount of double-counting when residents live and work in different provinces, vaccinations took place at work and both provinces count the vaccinations.)“ Free vaccines will be available to everyone in Canada over the course of 2021.” See government of Canada, CTV news websites, archived:  https://web.archive.org/web/20211119182257/https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/coronavirus-disease-covid-19/vaccines.html  https://web.archive.org/web/20211119184030/https://health-infobase.canada.ca/covid-19/vaccination-coverage/  https://web.archive.org/web/20211119162636/https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/news/2021/11/health-canada-authorizes-use-of-comirnaty-the-pfizer-biontech-covid-19-vaccine-in-children-5-to-11-years-of-age.html  https://web.archive.org/web/20211119182544/https://www.ctvnews.ca/health/coronavirus/covid-19-vaccine-booster-eligibility-by-province-and-territory-in-canada-1.5626554

column131: On 19 november 2021, the policy continues: “Federal public servants must be fully vaccinated … The criteria for being considered ‘fully vaccinated’ are based upon guidance from the Public Health Agency of Canada. column69: 20 november 2021 is the first full day in the province of New Brunswick (NB) that previous circuit-breaker restrictions on non-essential travel between NB regions no longer apply. This NB measure had applied to all – vaccinated and unvaccinated. NB and some other provinces continue to restrict entry from other jurisdictions by unvaccinated travellers. Effective 30 October 2021, the government of Canada began requiring all passengers “Boarding flights and trains …12 years of age plus 4 months, or older you’ll need to be fully vaccinated [or] … show a valid COVID-19 molecular test taken within 72 hours of travel.” There are no restrictions anywhere in Canada on domestic travel by unvaccinated persons. column74: On 26 november 2021, government of Canada Health and Transport Ministers announced “multiple restrictions on travel from countries in southern Africa, banning all foreign nationals who travelled there in the past 14 days and requiring anyone who has done so and is already in Canada to immediately go into quarantine… The countries affected by the travel ban are South Africa, Mozambique, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Lesotho, Eswatini and Namibia.” On 30 november 2021, the government of Canada “announced new measures to stem the spread of the Omicron variant in Canada, expanding a travel ban to include foreign nationals from Nigeria, Malawi and Egypt and adding testing requirements for travellers returning to Canada from anywhere in the world except the United States”. Canada remains open to entry by citizens of other countries, but for those “coming for a non-discretionary reason [open only] if you qualify as a fully vaccinated traveller”. In sum, the Canadian border is closed to all unvaccinated, non-essential foreign visitors. The Canadian border is open to fully vaccinated visitors from most countries, but is closed to even fully vaccinated foreign visitors from a list of African countries. See Globe and Mail and government of Canada websites, archived:  https://web.archive.org/web/20211128121638/https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-premiers-federal-conservatives-call-for-increased-travel-restrictions/  https://web.archive.org/web/20211129122810/https://travel.gc.ca/travel-covid/travel-restrictions/visitors-workers-students  https://web.archive.org/web/20211202122710/https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-ottawa-eyes-additional-measures-in-face-of-omicron-covid-19-variant/

column88: On 3 Dec. 2021, the government of Canada continues to advise: “Testing is the only way we can confirm if you have COVID-19. Knowing you're infected is important to protect your family and the people you encounter. Contact your local health authority for advice about testing if you think you may have COVID-19 (and/or) have been in contact with someone who has COVID-19.” Provincial, territorial and local public health agencies follow this guidance to test individuals who report possible symptoms or are possible contacts. Lateral flow tests (LFTs) have been approved by Health Canada. While lateral flow tests (LFTs) and other rapid tests are increasingly available to some asymptomatic people in some provinces, PCR testing of symptomatic individuals remains the standard first-test approach in the majority of cases in addition to being relied upon for final confirmation. Government of Canada data show that less than 20% of rapid tests distributed to provincial and territorial governments have been used. See Government of Canada websites, archived:  https://web.archive.org/web/20211203134551/https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/2019-novel-coronavirus-infection/symptoms/testing.html  https://web.archive.org/web/20211203140128/https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/2019-novel-coronavirus-infection/symptoms/testing/increased-supply.html

column106: On 3 december 2021 10:27AM EST, according to the CTV news unofficial vaccine tracker, 31,568,253 Canadians [83% of the total national population and 87% of the vaccine-eligible population aged 5+; note new definition of vax-eligible by age] have received at least one dose of an approved COVID-19 vaccine -- Moderna, Pfizer, Johnson & Johnson (J&J) Janssen, or AstraZeneca (AZ no longer recommended except in limited circumstances). 29,061,046 Canadians [76% of total pop. and 80% of vax-eligible aged 5+] are fully vaccinated against COVID-19 having received two doses. All provinces and territories are making vaccinations available to residents aged 5 and up. Vaccinations for those aged 5-11 just started this past week. (Note that vaccination data do not include Canadians who returned home after being vaccinated in other countries while wintering at retirement homes or on essential business trips. column88: On 13 Dec. 2021, the government of Canada continues to advise: “Testing is the only way we can confirm if you have COVID-19. Knowing you're infected is important to protect your family and the people you encounter. Contact your local health authority for advice about testing if you think you may have COVID-19 (and/or) have been in contact with someone who has COVID-19.” Provincial, territorial and local public health agencies follow this guidance to test individuals who report possible symptoms or are possible contacts. Lateral flow tests (LFTs) have been approved by Health Canada. Lateral flow tests (LFTs) and other rapid tests are increasingly available to some asymptomatic people in some provinces. According to recent newspaper reports: “Critics say some other jurisdictions, both in Canada and abroad, have made it much easier for people to get their hands on rapid tests for free …unlike in Ontario, Alberta or B.C…rapid antigen tests … are difficult to access … British Columbia, top doctor … said this week she’s not sure they are worth it”. Data show rapid test usage greater in some provinces without free access to rapid testing than in other provinces with free access. In some provinces, free access has not led to high usage perhaps because potential users have to take the initiative to pick up a free rapid test at a distribution centre vs. distribution in schools and workplaces in other provinces. Government of Canada data to end-November show that less than 20% of all 79,746,088 rapid tests distributed to provincial and territorial governments have been used (14,759,881). The Government of Canada’s Health Minister “said Ottawa would provide the provinces and territories with 35 million more rapid COVID-19 tests [almost 1 for every Canadian] even though tests provided to date remain “largely underutilized”. PCR testing of symptomatic individuals remains the standard first-test approach in the majority of cases in addition to being relied upon for final confirmation. column90: As of 13 december 2021, government of Canada advises that when individuals “test positive for COVID-19, a public health official will ask you questions to collect important information about your symptoms; activities and travel you did before you tested positive; all the people you may have been in close contact with while you were contagious ...contact tracing. It's a key public health measure.” Most provinces and territories continue to apply this advice. However, tracing capacity is not sufficient in some jurisdictions to deal with a surge in cases; e.g., in the province of Nova Scotia: “Public Health staff are experiencing a backlog in carrying out extended contact tracing due to the volume of  cases. Staff are helping people identified as initial contacts of positive cases to do their own contact tracing and encouraging people to isolate right away if they are a potential contact, rather than waiting for Public Health to get in touch.” See Governments of Canada and CBC news websites, archived:  https://web.archive.org/web/20211213214724/https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/2019-novel-coronavirus-infection/symptoms/testing.html  https://web.archive.org/web/20211213220028/https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/nova-scotia/dr-robert-strang-to-provide-st-fx-covid-19-update-1.6281419
column103: On 13 december 2021, the government of Canada advises: “Masks may be required or recommended in public settings like stores, schools, businesses, workplaces, public transit. Even if masks aren't required, you can still choose to wear one in shared spaces with people from outside of your immediate household. Whether you’re vaccinated or not, you should consider wearing one in shared spaces with people from outside of your immediate household. This is especially important indoors, whether in private or public settings. Masks are strongly recommended in any crowded setting, including settings with vaccination requirements.” All provinces and territories now have some requirement for masks in indoor public spaces. column106: On 13 december 2021 5:09PM EST, according to the CTV news unofficial vaccine tracker, 31,632,815 Canadians [83% of the total national population and 87% of the vaccine-eligible population aged 5+] have received at least one dose of an approved COVID-19 vaccine -- Moderna, Pfizer, Johnson & Johnson (J&J) Janssen, or AstraZeneca (AZ no longer recommended except in limited circumstances). 29,193,010 Canadians [76% of total pop. and 80% of vax-eligible aged 5+] are fully vaccinated against COVID-19 having received two doses. All provinces and territories are making vaccinations available to residents aged 5 and up. Vaccinations for those aged 5-11 just started at end-November. Provinces and territories are also delivering third doses to long-term care residents, immune-compromised patients, indigenous community residents, senior citizens and recipients of two earlier AZ doses based on national government guidance. The recommended age for third doses has just been lowered to those aged 50 and up. 2,441,379 third doses have been administered, which accounts for less than 7% of the national population. (Note that vaccination data do not include Canadians who returned home after being vaccinated in other countries while wintering at retirement homes or on essential business trips. On the other hand, there may be a small amount of double-counting when residents live and work in different provinces, vaccinations took place at work and both provinces count the vaccinations.)“ Free vaccines will be available to everyone in Canada over the course of 2021.” See government of Canada and CTV news websites, archived:  https://web.archive.org/web/20211211123912/https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/coronavirus-disease-covid-19/vaccines.html  https://web.archive.org/web/20211211124041/https://www.ctvnews.ca/health/coronavirus/covid-19-vaccine-booster-eligibility-by-province-and-territory-in-canada-1.5626554  https://web.archive.org/web/20211203160713/https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/phac-aspc/documents/services/immunization/national-advisory-committee-on-immunization-naci/guidance-booster-covid-19-vaccine-doses/guidance-booster-covid-19-vaccine-doses.pdf  https://web.archive.org/web/20211211124411/https://health-infobase.canada.ca/covid-19/vaccination-coverage/

column88: On 17 Dec. 2021, the government of Canada continues to advise: “Testing is the only way we can confirm if you have COVID-19. Contact your local health authority for advice about testing if you think you may have COVID-19 (and/or) have been in contact with someone who has COVID-19.” Provincial, territorial and local public health agencies follow this guidance to test individuals who report possible symptoms or are possible contacts. Lateral flow tests (LFTs) have been approved by Health Canada. In her Economic and Fiscal Statement 2021 (14 December), Canada’s Minister of Finance stated: “Access to rapid tests is an important tool for breaking paths of transmission—including against emerging variants of concern ... The government proposes to provide $1.7 billion to Health Canada and the Public Health Agency of Canada to continue supporting provinces and territories in securing the rapid testing supplies they need to keep Canadians safe and healthy, including through expanded school and workplace testing programs. This funding would also support the procurement of additional rapid test kits for distribution to Canadians.”  Provinces and territories intend to make lateral flow tests (LFTs) and other rapid tests increasingly available to asymptomatic people. However, Government of Canada data show that less than 20% of all 81,575,467 rapid tests distributed to provincial and territorial governments as well as the military, federal prisons, the Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC), and Northern, remote and Indigenous communities have been used (15,509,620). Some provinces are just starting mass distribution of rapid tests and have not yet solved how to get tests to potential users. If you're not in those cities, you can access testing kits through Alberta Health Services sites…Rapid test kits will also be made available at more schools and for vulnerable populations. The kits are intended for people without symptoms of COVID-19.” In Quebec, “rapid tests … are to be distributed to the general public via pharmacies starting Monday [20 Dec.]” PCR testing of symptomatic individuals remains the standard first-test approach in the majority of cases in addition to being relied upon for final confirmation. column106: On 17 december 2021 11:07AM EST, according to the CTV news unofficial vaccine tracker, 31,164,644 Canadians [81.5% of the total national population and 86% of the vaccine-eligible population aged 5+; NOTE correction to previous estimates “to remove doses that were being double-counted” by two provinces] have received at least one dose of an approved COVID-19 vaccine -- Moderna, Pfizer, Johnson & Johnson (J&J) Janssen, or AstraZeneca (AZ no longer recommended except in limited circumstances). 29,256,463 Canadians [76.5% of total pop. and 80.5% of vax-eligible aged 5+] are fully vaccinated against COVID-19 having received two doses. All provinces and territories are making vaccinations available to residents aged 5 and up. Vaccinations for those aged 5-11 just started at end-November. Provinces and territories are also delivering third doses to long-term care residents, immune-compromised patients, indigenous community residents, senior citizens and recipients of two earlier AZ doses based on national government guidance. The Government-of-Canada-recommended age for third doses has been lowered to those aged 50 and up. Some provinces have lowered the third-dose eligibility age to 18. 3,858,466 third doses have been administered, or about 10% of the national population. (Note that vaccination data do not include Canadians who returned home after being vaccinated in other countries while wintering at retirement homes or on essential business trips. On the other hand, there may be a small amount of double-counting when residents live and work in different provinces, vaccinations took place at work and both provinces count the vaccinations.) “Free vaccines will be available to everyone in Canada over the course of 2021.” See government of Canada and CTV news websites, archived:  https://web.archive.org/web/20211217150658/https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/coronavirus-disease-covid-19/vaccines.html  https://web.archive.org/web/20211217171512/https://www.ctvnews.ca/health/coronavirus/coronavirus-vaccination-tracker-how-many-people-in-canada-have-received-shots-1.5247509  https://web.archive.org/web/20211217151228/https://www.ctvnews.ca/health/coronavirus/covid-19-vaccine-booster-eligibility-by-province-and-territory-in-canada  https://web.archive.org/web/20211203160713/https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/phac-aspc/documents/services/immunization/national-advisory-committee-on-immunization-naci/guidance-booster-covid-19-vaccine-doses/guidance-booster-covid-19-vaccine-doses.pdf
column119: As of 17 december 2021, eligibility continues to be 5 years of age and up in all provinces and territories consistent with national government guidance. Based on national government guidance, provinces and territories are also delivering third doses to long-term care residents, immune-compromised patients, indigenous community residents, those aged 50 and up and recipients of two earlier AstraZeneca (AZ) doses. (AZ no longer used in Canada.) Some provinces have lowered the third-dose eligibility age to 18. See government of Canada and CTV news websites, archived:  https://web.archive.org/web/20211217150658/https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/coronavirus-disease-covid-19/vaccines.html  https://web.archive.org/web/20211203160713/https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/phac-aspc/documents/services/immunization/national-advisory-committee-on-immunization-naci/guidance-booster-covid-19-vaccine-doses/guidance-booster-covid-19-vaccine-doses.pdf  https://web.archive.org/web/20211217151228/https://www.ctvnews.ca/health/coronavirus/covid-19-vaccine-booster-eligibility-by-province-and-territory-in-canada

column74: Effective 19 december 2021, Canada is open to entry by citizens of all countries: “you can enter Canada if you qualify as a fully vaccinated traveller or you’re coming for a non-optional purpose” and “foreign nationals who had recently visited Botswana, Egypt, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa and Zimbabwe will no longer be barred from entering Canada”. “Fully vaccinated travellers must also meet all other entry criteria, including: submitting all required COVID-19 information into ArriveCAN prior to travel …being asymptomatic upon arrival; having a paper or digital copy of your proof of vaccination …; and having a suitable quarantine plan, in case it is required. Within 72 hours before your arrival to Canada or prior to scheduled departure of flight to Canada: Take a pre-entry COVID-19 molecular test (Antigen tests are not accepted for entry) or have proof of a positive test result received in the previous 14-180 days…After entry (coming from any country other than the U.S. in the past 14 days) Quarantine until receipt of your negative arrival test. Answer compliance verification calls from the Government of Canada …If you test positive or develop symptoms, you are required to isolate for 10 days from the time the test result is received, or the start of symptoms. You also need to contact the Public Health Agency of Canada”. In sum, the Canadian border is closed to all unvaccinated, non-essential foreign visitors. The Canadian border is open to fully vaccinated foreign visitors. Americans are subject to screening requirements. Non-Americans are subject to quarantine until they receive a negative covid test administered on arrival. See Government of Canada and Toronto Star websites, archived:  https://web.archive.org/web/20211226133101/https://www.thestar.com/politics/federal/2021/12/17/canada-lifts-african-travel-bans-restores-covid-19-pre-arrival-tests-for-short-trips.html  https://web.archive.org/web/20211217143745/https://travel.gc.ca/travel-covid/travel-restrictions/visitors-workers-students  https://web.archive.org/web/20220128161010/https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/publications/diseases-conditions/fully-vaccinated-travellers-entering-canada-covid-19.html

column103: Effective 20 december 2021, the government of Quebec revokes the mask exemption for students in secondary school classes: “Wearing a procedural mask is required at all times inside the school.” All provinces and territories now require masks in indoor public spaces consistent with Government of Canada advice: “Masks may be required or recommended in public settings like stores, schools, businesses, workplaces, public transit. Even if masks aren't required, you can still choose to wear one in shared spaces with people from outside of your immediate household. Whether you’re vaccinated or not, you should consider wearing one in shared spaces with people from outside of your immediate household. This is especially important indoors, whether in private or public settings. Masks are strongly recommended in any crowded setting, including settings with vaccination requirements.” See Governments of Canada and Quebec as well as Retail Council of Canada websites, archived:  https://web.archive.org/web/20211229211849/https://cdn-contenu.quebec.ca/cdn-contenu/adm/min/education/publications-adm/covid-19/consignes-scolaire-AN.pdf?1639771611  https://web.archive.org/web/20211217145353/https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/2019-novel-coronavirus-infection/prevention-risks/about-non-medical-masks-face-coverings.html  https://web.archive.org/web/20211217145713/https://www.retailcouncil.org/coronavirus-info-for-retailers/provincial-reopening-frameworks/  https://web.archive.org/web/20211217145838/https://www.retailcouncil.org/coronavirus-info-for-retailers/mask-requirements-affecting-retailers/

column88: On 23 Dec. 2021, the Chief Public Health Officer of Canada continues to advise that “a vaccines plus approach continues to be essential to the pandemic response in Canada. This includes … getting tested if symptomatic and/or as recommended”. The current policy intent of most provinces and territories is to supplement polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of symptomatic cases with mass availability of lateral flow and other rapid tests. However the caseload wave is frustrating efforts to achieve testing goals: ‘Faced with a tidal wave of COVID-19 cases, health officials in Alberta and in Montreal are asking residents to rely on rapid home test kits rather than line up for the more reliable PCR lab tests. Alberta axed general access to PCR tests on Thursday, despite the widespread shortage of rapid test kits. The province’s Chief Medical Officer of Health … asked those with forthcoming PRC test appointments to cancel them … [and] said the province dialled back PCR access to conserve the more accurate tests for high-risk groups, such health care workers, continuing-care residents, and those who qualify for antibody treatment because of their clinical condition. “As Omicron is spreading …, no one in Canada will be able to maintain PCR testing for every community case with mild symptoms” … Alberta did not require residents using rapid tests to report a positive result. The province will still track severe outcomes, such as death [and] will also monitor the prevalence of COVID-19 with other tools, such as wastewater data…Montreal public-health director … said Montrealers who get a positive result from a rapid antigen test … need not undertake another screening to confirm their status…the local health authority … around Vancouver has begun rationing PCR tests … only people deemed by medical experts to be “at greater risk of severe disease from COVID-19? are being given these tests on site.” See government of Canada and Globe and Mail newspaper websites, archived:    https://web.archive.org/web/20211227131740/https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/news/2021/12/statement-from-the-chief-public-health-officer-of-canada-on-december-23-2021.html  https://web.archive.org/web/20211227131413/https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-alberta-montreal-call-to-scale-back-pcr-lab-testing-as-demand-rises/  https://web.archive.org/web/20211227132009/https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-ontario-lab-professionals-working-beyond-humanly-possible-to-process/  https://web.archive.org/web/20211227132501/https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/article-provinces-working-to-meet-demand-for-covid-19-testing-as-cases-surge/

column24: On 24 December 2021, in Nunavut Territory: “Effective immediately, in every Nunavut community: All non-essential businesses and government offices are closed. Bars and licensed establishments are closed. Restaurants may open for takeout only.” In the rest of Canada, businesses are open with varying levels of restrictions. Many jurisdictions restrict access to some non-essential businesses to fully vaccinated customers (or require proof of a recent negative test). See Retail Council of Canada as well as governments of Nunavut websites,   https://web.archive.org/web/20211225214240/https://gov.nu.ca/health/news/new-covid-cases-lead-nunavut-wide-restrictions  https://web.archive.org/web/20211225215037/https://www.retailcouncil.org/coronavirus-info-for-retailers/vaccination-requirements-by-province/

column60: Effective 31 december 2021: the province of “Quebec’s government is imposing a nighttime curfew that will begin on New Year’s Eve in an attempt to reduce the high transmission of COVID-19 across the province and ease pressure on the hospital network.
